EXPL-FR: Explaining Face Recognition Models via Vision-Language Alignment

Guray Ozgur Affiliation: Fraunhofer IGD, Fraunhoferstr. 5, 64283 Darmstadt, Germany Affiliation: TU Darmstadt, Karolinenpl. 5, 64289 Darmstadt, Germany    Mustafa Tamyapar Affiliation: Fraunhofer IGD, Fraunhoferstr. 5, 64283 Darmstadt, Germany Affiliation: TU Darmstadt, Karolinenpl. 5, 64289 Darmstadt, Germany    Naser Damer Affiliation: Fraunhofer IGD, Fraunhoferstr. 5, 64283 Darmstadt, Germany Affiliation: TU Darmstadt, Karolinenpl. 5, 64289 Darmstadt, Germany    Fadi Boutros Affiliation: Fraunhofer IGD, Fraunhoferstr. 5, 64283 Darmstadt, Germany
Abstract

Deep face recognition (FR) models reach near-saturated accuracy but remain opaque: a practitioner cannot ask which semantic attributes a similarity score relied upon. EXPL-FR answers this inside the FR model’s own embedding space. A lightweight adapter aligns a vision-language model’s (VLM) image encoder with the frozen FR space, trained on face images alone and never on text. Because the VLM’s encoders share one space, the same adapter applies to the text encoder, turning 978 attribute prompts in 22 categories, also extendable, into FR-space anchors at no extra cost. We do not assume this transfer works: a face-verification protocol measures it, and an ablation changing only the adapter isolates its contribution. Not every concept survives, because an FR model earns its invariances by discarding the factors it must verify identities across. A label-free detectability measure compares each concept’s separability in FR space against the VLM space, and the 100 most detectable form the model’s readable semantic signature, which separates identities better than the full vocabulary. We cover four FR backbones and two VLM encoders, EXPL-FR needs no architecture access, and supports identity-level, per-image, and differential explanations. We benchmark attribute-level auditing under three supervision settings, human labels (current practice), VLM pseudo-labels, and our fully prompt-driven audit, against real verification behavior. With no labels, the prompt-driven audit ranks four FR models by their measured per-ethnicity RFW errors and ranks controlled attribute changes by their true verification cost.

Face Recognition Explainability Vision-Language Models

1 Introduction

Face recognition (FR) systems are deployed at borders, on devices, and in access control, where one verification decision carries legal, financial, or safety consequences [43, 49, 1]. Modern models [8, 2, 35, 25, 26], trained with margin-based losses on web-scale identity data [14, 59], report near-saturated accuracy [16, 36, 41, 56, 57] yet remain opaque: a practitioner gets a similarity score and no way to ask why, at odds with demands for transparency in biometrics [46, 20, 21, 17, 19, 18]. Prior explainable FR (XFR) work addresses this spatially or geometrically, mapping where a matcher focused or how invariant it is to a small, pre-chosen attribute set [40, 51, 31, 27, 45, 9, 10, 7, 38, 29], explaining what a model relies upon instead requires connecting its embedding space to an open, human-specified vocabulary. VLMs such as CLIP [39] are the natural source of such a vocabulary, but prior work either routes classifier decisions through VLM concepts [28, 52, 54, 37, 24, 12], requiring a decision layer a deployed FR encoder lacks, or adapts a frozen CLIP to FR-adjacent tasks purely for performance [13, 55, 32, 5, 6, 58]. The missing piece, a strictly post-hoc bridge from language into an already-frozen FR space, is nontrivial: independently trained encoders are not guaranteed compatible and a single VLM’s own encoders are imperfectly aligned (the modality gap [30]), though independently trained vision models do increasingly converge [22, 11].

EXPL-FR closes this gap with a lightweight adapter aligning a frozen VLM’s image space with a frozen FR encoder’s space, trained on face images only and never on text. Two empirical findings carry the paper. First, the image-only adapter transfers to the text encoder almost for free: the encoders share one pretrained space, so pushing a prompt through the same adapter gives a usable proxy for where that concept sits in FR space, turning an arbitrary vocabulary into a bank of FR-space semantic anchors without touching the FR model’s internals. Second, an FR model earns its invariances, discarding exactly the factors it must verify identities across, so only some concepts stay detectable after the mapping, a label-free measure contrasting FR- against VLM-space separability identifies each model’s identity-discriminating attributes, whose coordinates form its semantic signature. This keep/discount structure is the object of study: it is what explanations should be read over, and what attribute-level auditing measures, an analysis that until now required labels or a controllable generator. Our contributions: (i) EXPL-FR, to our knowledge the first framework aligning a frozen, black-box FR embedding space with a frozen VLM through an image-side adapter whose alignment transfers zero-shot to text, giving a human-readable semantic signature for any face without training on text, (ii) a face-verification protocol validating that transfer as a faithful proxy for the FR identity space across several FR architectures and VLM backbones, plus a label-free detectability measure whose top-100100 attributes define the signature and beat the full vocabulary at identity separation, (iii) per-image, identity-level, and genuine/imposter/morph-differential explanations, with no retraining and no white-box access, (iv) an attribute-level auditing benchmark under three supervision settings, labeled (prior practice), VLM-proxy, and fully prompt-driven (ours), validated against real verification behavior on RFW, GAN-Control, and CelebA, quantifying the trade-off between supervision cost and audit quality.

2 Related Work

Explainable FR. Most XFR methods localize decisions spatially rather than semantically: saliency scored by inpainting [51], patch-pair decompositions of the cosine score [31], or neurons paired with a hand-annotated “Face Dictionary” [45]. Each explains where the matcher looked and needs an image pair, gradients, or a concept set tied to one architecture, none expresses evidence as similarity to a freely chosen textual concept. Other lines make decisions transparent without naming attributes: similarity-score backpropagation marks the pixels arguing for and against a match [20], score uncertainty and decision confidence say how far a match can be trusted [21], and explanations have moved off the spatial axis into the frequency domain [18]. Each reports where, in which band, or how confidently, never which named attribute. Closest to us, Leroy et al. [29] characterize how attributes shape FR embedding geometry, but need supervision throughout: per-image labels (CelebA’s 4040), a controllable generator (GAN-Control), and a vocabulary limited to what those annotations cover. We remove that dependency, taking axes from text so any unlabeled collection will do and a new attribute costs one written prompt, and we add instance-level explanations an aggregate analysis cannot give. We run the same analysis with labels, pseudo-labels, and prompts alone (Section 3.5). VLMs: concepts, tasks, decisions. Concept-bottleneck and probing approaches [28, 52, 54, 37, 24, 12] explain classifiers through named concepts but require a decision layer, which an FR encoder, a feature extractor, does not offer. Closest in mechanism is LaVMD [23], which likewise aligns a VLM to a target model and probes it with text, but targets a classifier: alignment is anchored on a shared classification head over a closed label set, and the output diagnoses which subgroups that classifier gets wrong. A deployed FR encoder offers neither, only extracted features that EXPL-FR couples with the explanations. Adapter methods [13, 55] and face-centric instances [32, 5, 6, 58] adapt CLIP within its own space, not providing any explanations. LLM-based explanations of FR decisions [9, 10, 7, 38, 44, 15] reason over landmarks, chat prompts, or a separate model’s judgment, and state the outcome in natural language, but all explain in the vision-language model’s space: a second model describes the faces rather than the matcher. EXPL-FR reads the deployed FR encoder’s own coordinates, so its explanations answer for the matcher itself. Cross-model alignment. Our transfer depends on the imperfect coupling between representation convergence across independently trained models [22, 11] and the modality gap within a single VLM [30].

3 Methodology

EXPL-FR has four steps: train one small adapter mapping VLM image embeddings onto FR embeddings, from face images only (Section 3.2), apply that same adapter to text, turning every prompt into an FR-space direction (Section 3.3), keep the prompts that remain detectable, whose coordinates form the semantic signature (Section 3.3), and read signatures to explain data (Section 3.4) and audit models (Section 3.5). Only the adapter is trained, both encoders stay frozen.

3.1 Setup: Two Frozen Encoders and a Semantic Vocabulary

We fix a vocabulary of KK short prompts 𝒯={t1,…,tK}\mathcal{T}=\{t_{1},\dots,t_{K}\} in MM disjoint categories 𝒞={c1,…,cM}\mathcal{C}=\{c_{1},\dots,c_{M}\} covering the axes along which two face images commonly vary. Each attribute is a single-concept template prompt (e.g. “A photo of a person wearing {eyewear}.”), one value per prompt, single-concept describes the phrasing, not the visual factor, since a hair-style prompt still carries length, volume, and texture, so readings are directional rather than disentangled. The vocabulary is fixed once and reused unchanged across every FR model, VLM, and dataset, so signatures under different encoders share a common basis.

Let ϕv:ℝH×W×3→ℝd\phi_{v}:\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times 3}\to\mathbb{R}^{d} and ϕt:ℒ→ℝd\phi_{t}:\mathcal{L}\to\mathbb{R}^{d} be the frozen VLM image and text encoders, sharing a dd-dimensional space by their contrastive pretraining, and ψ:ℝH′×W′×3→ℝdFR\psi:\mathbb{R}^{H^{\prime}\times W^{\prime}\times 3}\to\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{FR}}} the frozen FR encoder. All embeddings are ℓ2\ell_{2}-normalized,

𝐞¯v=ϕv​(𝐱)∥ϕv​(𝐱)∥2,𝐞¯tk=ϕt​(tk)∥ϕt​(tk)∥2,𝐟¯=ψ⁡(𝐱)∥ψ⁡(𝐱)∥2,\bar{\mathbf{e}}_{v}=\frac{\phi_{v}(\mathbf{x})}{\lVert\phi_{v}(\mathbf{x})\rVert_{2}},\qquad\bar{\mathbf{e}}_{t}^{k}=\frac{\phi_{t}(t_{k})}{\lVert\phi_{t}(t_{k})\rVert_{2}},\qquad\bar{\mathbf{f}}=\frac{\psi(\mathbf{x})}{\lVert\psi(\mathbf{x})\rVert_{2}},\vskip-2.84526pt (1)

so all inner products are cosines. Only the adapter is ever learned.

3.2 Image-Only Alignment: Can Two Frozen Spaces Be Bridged?

The VLM image space and the FR space are not aligned a priori (ϕv\phi_{v} optimizes visual-semantic grounding, ψ\psi identity discrimination), which is what makes the problem hard: a prompt embedding and an FR embedding are simply vectors in two unrelated coordinate systems, so their cosine carries no meaning and no concept can be named inside the FR space without first relating the two. We bridge them with a lightweight adapter gθ:ℝd→ℝdFRg_{\theta}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{FR}}}. Data. Paired frozen embeddings 𝒟align={(𝐞¯vi,𝐟¯i)}i=1N\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{align}}=\{(\bar{\mathbf{e}}_{v}^{i},\bar{\mathbf{f}}_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N} over a large identity-labeled dataset, face images only, never attribute labels or text. Objective. A cosine alignment loss,

ℒ⁡(θ)=1N​∑i=1N(1−⟨gθ​(𝐞¯vi)¯,𝐟¯i⟩),gθ​(𝐞)¯=gθ​(𝐞)∥gθ​(𝐞)∥2,\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left(1-\left\langle\overline{g_{\theta}(\bar{\mathbf{e}}_{v}^{i})},\ \bar{\mathbf{f}}_{i}\right\rangle\right),\qquad\overline{g_{\theta}(\mathbf{e})}=\frac{g_{\theta}(\mathbf{e})}{\lVert g_{\theta}(\mathbf{e})\rVert_{2}},\vskip-5.69054pt (2)

driving the normalized output toward the target direction without penalizing magnitude, since decisions come from angular distance. Architecture. A 44-layer MLP: three blocks (bias-free linear, BatchNorm, GELU) then a linear with bias, the first layer mapping ℝd→ℝdFR\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{FR}}} (asymmetric when d≠dFRd\neq d_{\mathrm{FR}}) and the rest staying in ℝdFR\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{FR}}}: ≈1.05\approx\!1.05M parameters at 512→512512{\to}512 (1.181.18M at 768→512768{\to}512), orders of magnitude below either encoder. Optimization (Section 4.1). Each epoch the current ϕv→gθ\phi_{v}\!\to\!g_{\theta} pipeline is plugged into held-out 1:1 verification and the best-mean-accuracy checkpoint kept, measuring how much of ψ\psi’s identity structure the adapter recovers. Why this direction? One could instead map FR embeddings into the VLM space, where alignment with text holds by construction. But the FR space is the object of study: every quantity we report is defined on FR embeddings, and the VLM space discards identity. Worse, comparing faces and concepts inside the VLM space would make the readout the VLM’s own image-text similarity with a learned layer inserted: nothing would be attributable to ψ\psi.

3.3 Zero-Shot Transfer to Text: Anchors and Signatures

gθg_{\theta} is trained exclusively on paired image embeddings and never sees text, but it is simply a learned function on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, and a prompt’s embedding 𝐞¯tk\bar{\mathbf{e}}_{t}^{k} lives in that same space. We therefore hypothesize that gθg_{\theta} maps a concept’s text embedding into FR space consistently with how it maps images of that concept:

𝐩k=gθ​(𝐞¯tk)∥gθ​(𝐞¯tk)∥2,k=1,…,K,\mathbf{p}_{k}=\frac{g_{\theta}(\bar{\mathbf{e}}_{t}^{k})}{\lVert g_{\theta}(\bar{\mathbf{e}}_{t}^{k})\rVert_{2}},\qquad k=1,\dots,K,\vskip-5.69054pt (3)

Nothing supervises this transfer, so Section 4.2 measures what survives it. Projecting a face’s FR embedding onto every candidate anchor yields the vocabulary projection,

sk​(𝐱)=⟨𝐟¯,𝐩k⟩,𝐬⁡(𝐱)=[s1​(𝐱),…,sK​(𝐱)]⊤∈ℝK,s^{k}(\mathbf{x})=\left\langle\bar{\mathbf{f}},\mathbf{p}_{k}\right\rangle,\qquad\mathbf{s}(\mathbf{x})=\left[s^{1}(\mathbf{x}),\dots,s^{K}(\mathbf{x})\right]^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{K},\vskip-5.69054pt (4)

every coordinate of which reads through its prompt. Not every coordinate deserves to be read, however. Selecting the signature: identity-discriminating attributes. An FR model earns its invariances: to verify identities across pose, expression, lighting, and capture conditions it must discard those factors, so some concepts land on directions along which the FR space no longer separates faces, and the full projection mixes coordinates the model encodes with coordinates it has erased. We measure which, per prompt and label-free, on an unlabeled, identity-disjoint collection. The VLM’s centered grounding score rk​(𝐱)=⟨𝐞¯v​(𝐱),𝐞¯tk−𝝁t¯⟩r_{k}(\mathbf{x})=\langle\bar{\mathbf{e}}_{v}(\mathbf{x}),\overline{\bar{\mathbf{e}}_{t}^{k}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{t}}\rangle (𝝁t\boldsymbol{\mu}_{t} the vocabulary-mean text embedding) pseudo-labels each prompt’s extremes, a mean-difference detector is fit on one identity half and scored on the other, once among the VLM image embeddings (AUCVk\mathrm{AUC}_{V}^{k}) and once among the adapter-mapped ones (AUCFk\mathrm{AUC}_{F}^{k}). Both are scored against the VLM’s own pseudo-labels, so they quantify pseudo-label separability, not the verified presence of a concept. AUCV\mathrm{AUC}_{V} is near-saturated structurally: its labels are the extremes of a direction in the very space it is measured in, so a high value shows self-consistency, not that the VLM has grounded the concept. We adopt it knowingly: without per-image labels the VLM’s image-text coupling is the only way to name concepts at vocabulary scale, and what it cannot rank bounds the whole framework. The drop AUCVk−AUCFk\mathrm{AUC}_{V}^{k}-\mathrm{AUC}_{F}^{k} therefore upper-bounds the discount of concept kk, read as a ranking over prompts, not absolute levels. AUCF\mathrm{AUC}_{F} is itself read on adapter-mapped embeddings, hence conservative, Section 4.3 measures that bias against true FR embeddings and finds the real discount larger, never smaller. We nonetheless select on it, because selection asks a different question from measurement: the anchor 𝐩k\mathbf{p}_{k} is an adapter output, so a concept the FR space separates but no prompt can aim at is useless for a language-grounded signature. AUCF\mathrm{AUC}_{F} scores detectability along exactly the directions the anchors occupy, ranking prompts by detectable and reachable. The identity-discriminating attributes, a name chosen so that the FR space still separates faces along the attribute, not that the attribute determines identity or drives the match (Section 4.3), 𝒦ψ⊂𝒯\mathcal{K}_{\psi}\subset\mathcal{T} are the top-mm prompts by AUCFk\mathrm{AUC}_{F}^{k}. The semantic signature of 𝐱\mathbf{x} under ψ\psi is Eq. 4 restricted to 𝒦ψ\mathcal{K}_{\psi}, with m=100m{=}100 throughout (validated in Section 4.3). The discounted complement is not discarded knowledge: which concepts a model keeps versus discounts is what the audits of Section 3.5 measure.

3.4 Using Signatures: Explaining Data, Auditing Models

Because attribute axes are synthesized from text, every analysis below is label-free: face images only, no per-image labels, no controllable generator, the key practical difference from [29]. Two orthogonal axes follow: fix the FR model and vary the data (this subsection), or fix the data and vary the model (Section 3.5). Explanations read the coordinates in 𝒦ψ\mathcal{K}_{\psi}, since a coordinate the model has discounted cannot explain its decision. Per-image: ranking the coordinates by magnitude surfaces the prompts ψ\psi represents the face as most aligned with. Identity-wise: aggregating over an identity’s enrolled images reveals the categories the model consistently associates with that identity. Differential: for a pair, Δk=sk​(𝐱a)−sk​(𝐱b)\Delta^{k}=s^{k}(\mathbf{x}_{a})-s^{k}(\mathbf{x}_{b}) isolates the axes along which ψ\psi separates them, small and unstructured against a genuine image but large against an imposter or morph, exposing which attributes drive rejection.

3.5 Auditing FR Models: Supervision Levels

No prompt of 𝒯\mathcal{T} is used while an adapter is trained, so any concept can be measured afterwards. Auditing differs from explanation in what it reads: explanations use only the kept coordinates, whereas an audit measures every candidate concept, since how strongly a model structures an attribute is the audit’s subject, and Section 4.4 shows that pattern predicts real verification behavior. Every audit has three steps: construct an FR-space axis for a named concept, measure a statistic along it, validate it against real behavior. Only the construction differs, giving three supervision settings. (1) Labels, prior practice. Annotations yi∈{0,1}y_{i}\in\{0,1\} select the two groups directly in FR space and the axis is the normalized difference of FR-embedding means, 𝐚^(1)∝meanyi=1𝐟¯i−meanyi=0𝐟¯i\hat{\mathbf{a}}^{(1)}\propto\mathop{\mathrm{mean}}_{y_{i}=1}\bar{\mathbf{f}}_{i}-\mathop{\mathrm{mean}}_{y_{i}=0}\bar{\mathbf{f}}_{i} (one-vs-rest for categorical attributes): the supervision [29] requires, and our upper bound. (2) VLM-proxy. The VLM’s image-text coupling replaces annotation: each prompt ranks an unlabeled collection by rkr_{k} (Section 3.3), the top- and bottom-qq quantile sets Hk+,Hk−H_{k}^{+},H_{k}^{-} stand in for the labeled groups, and the axis is the mean difference of (1),

𝐚^(2)∝mean𝐱∈Hk+𝐟¯​(𝐱)−mean𝐱∈Hk−𝐟¯​(𝐱),\hat{\mathbf{a}}^{(2)}\propto\mathop{\mathrm{mean}}_{\mathbf{x}\in H_{k}^{+}}\bar{\mathbf{f}}(\mathbf{x})\,-\mathop{\mathrm{mean}}_{\mathbf{x}\in H_{k}^{-}}\bar{\mathbf{f}}(\mathbf{x}),\vskip-5.69054pt (5)

This is the natural label-free baseline: no annotations, only prompts and unlabeled images. (3) Prompt axis, ours. No labels, and no images at construction. For a probed attribute, a small ordered prompt set (e.g. “a photo of a baby” →…→\to\dots\to “a photo of an elderly person”, L≥2L\geq 2) is mapped by the same adapter, and the axis is

𝐚^(3)=PC1​({gθ​(𝐞¯tℓ)¯}ℓ=1L),\hat{\mathbf{a}}^{(3)}=\mathrm{PC}_{1}\!\left(\left\{\overline{g_{\theta}(\bar{\mathbf{e}}_{t}^{\ell})}\right\}_{\ell=1}^{L}\right), (6)

where 𝐞¯tℓ\bar{\mathbf{e}}_{t}^{\ell} is the ℓ\ell-th prompt’s text embedding, gθ​(⋅)¯\overline{g_{\theta}(\cdot)} the normalized adapter output of Eq. 2, and PC1​(⋅)\mathrm{PC}_{1}(\cdot) the first principal direction of the point set, reducing to the normalized difference of the two points when L=2L=2, its sign points from the first prompt toward the last. For a categorical group the axis instead runs from the FR population mean, computed once on the adapter’s identity holdout, toward the group’s mapped prompt-set mean, so no image is touched at construction. For probed attributes the axis depends only on how the adapter separates the prompts from each other, never on any single mapped prompt, so a new attribute costs one written sentence or a few phrasings. Audits are never restricted to 𝒦ψ\mathcal{K}_{\psi}, because invariances self-report: every statistic below is a projection onto a unit axis, so an invariance (Δ=𝐟¯​(𝐱+)−𝐟¯​(𝐱−)≈𝟎\Delta=\bar{\mathbf{f}}(\mathbf{x}^{+})-\bar{\mathbf{f}}(\mathbf{x}^{-})\approx\mathbf{0}) reads as a small value wherever the axis points, and that is the finding. The four statistics, identical across settings. Each setting yields a unit axis 𝐚^(s)\hat{\mathbf{a}}^{(s)}, and every statistic starts from the same projection v⁡(𝐱)=⟨𝐟¯​(𝐱),𝐚^(s)⟩v(\mathbf{x})=\langle\bar{\mathbf{f}}(\mathbf{x}),\hat{\mathbf{a}}^{(s)}\rangle, so the settings differ only in how the axis was built. Dependence asks how strongly a concept structures the FR space: the analysis images are split into two groups along the concept, and the two-sample KS statistic between the within-group and across-group FR distance distributions measures the effect on the geometry, following [29]. Setting (1) takes the groups from labels yiy_{i}, settings (2)-(3) take the top- and bottom-K′K^{\prime} images ranked by vv, so any unlabeled collection qualifies. Profile is the same statistic over the whole vocabulary, a per-category fingerprint, its groups are ranked by rkr_{k} rather than vv, making them identical for every FR model, so profile differences reflect FR geometry alone. Sensitivity asks how far a controlled change of one attribute moves the embedding along the axis named for it, |⟨Δ,𝐚^(s)⟩||\langle\Delta,\hat{\mathbf{a}}^{(s)}\rangle|, with Δ\Delta the embedding difference between traversal endpoints. Attribution asks whether the largest such projection is the attribute actually varied, as top-1 accuracy against eight competitors. Axes are always built on images, or for traversals on identities, disjoint from those analyzed. Section 4.4 validates dependence against real verification error and sensitivity against real EER. Validation: three questions, conditioned statistics. A pooled correlation over all (model, attribute) pairs conflates attribute with model variance, so we condition. Fixing the attribute and rank-correlating models against real behavior answers model selection (which model should I deploy?), fixing the model and rank-correlating attributes answers model diagnosis (which variations will cost it?), where no per-attribute ground truth exists, agreement with the supervised audit (1) measures how well the label-free settings replace it. Real behavior comes from attribute-isolating verification protocols and per-subset accuracy. Validating faithfulness via face verification. A signature is only useful if it reflects the identity information in ψ⁡(𝐱)\psi(\mathbf{x}), we quantify this with the standard 1:1 protocol under eight representations, each isolating one component: (1) ψ↔ψ\psi{\leftrightarrow}\psi (FR upper bound), (2) ϕv↔ϕv\phi_{v}{\leftrightarrow}\phi_{v} (raw VLM identity), (3) gθ​(ϕv)↔gθ​(ϕv)g_{\theta}(\phi_{v}){\leftrightarrow}g_{\theta}(\phi_{v}) (does the adapter preserve it?), (4) ϕv↔ψ\phi_{v}{\leftrightarrow}\psi (unaligned lower bound), (5) gθ​(ϕv)↔ψg_{\theta}(\phi_{v}){\leftrightarrow}\psi (alignment quality), (6) 𝐬⁡(𝐱)\mathbf{s}(\mathbf{x}) with anchors left unaligned (𝐩k=𝐞¯tk\mathbf{p}_{k}=\bar{\mathbf{e}}_{t}^{k}, the vocabulary’s own identity signal), (7) 𝐬⁡(𝐱)\mathbf{s}(\mathbf{x}) with the anchors of Eq. 3, (8) as (7) with 𝐟¯\bar{\mathbf{f}} replaced by gθ​(𝐞¯v)¯\overline{g_{\theta}(\bar{\mathbf{e}}_{v})}, no FR forward pass at inference. 4 Results

4.1 Experimental Setup

Semantic vocabulary. K=978K{=}978 prompts in M=22M{=}22 categories, from demographics (gender, age, ethnicity) through hair, expression, facial features, and make-up to eyewear, headwear, lighting, and scene context. Vision-language model. Unless noted, ϕv,ϕt\phi_{v},\phi_{t} are the frozen encoders of CLIP ViT-B/16 [39] (d=512d{=}512), we additionally evaluate SigLIP [47] (d=768d{=}768). FR targets. Primary: AdaFace [25] ViT-B/WebFace4M [59] (dFR=512d_{\mathrm{FR}}{=}512), for generality (Table 1), adapters are also aligned against AdaFace ViT-S/WebFace4M, ResNet-100/WebFace4M, and ResNet-100/MS1MV2 [14]. Adapter training. gθg_{\theta} is aligned on WebFace4M with an identity-disjoint 10%10\% holdout, Adam, lr 10−310^{-3} with cosine annealing, weight decay 10−410^{-4}, batch 10241024, 5050 epochs, common setting for every FR target and VLM. Those same held-out identities also serve as the unlabeled pool for the detectability measure (Section 3.3), so concepts are selected on identities no adapter has trained on. Evaluation protocols [8, 2, 25]: 1010-fold 1:11{:}1 verification accuracy (%) on LFW [16], AgeDB-30 [36], CFP-FP [41], CPLFW [56], CALFW [57] with their mean (which also selects adapter checkpoints), TAR@FAR=10−4{=}10^{-4} (%) on IJB-B/C [50, 34], rank-1 identification (%) on TinyFace [3]. Explanation showcase data. Figure 1b: 22 random CASIA-WebFace [53] identities, 5050 images each. Figure 1c,d: reference/genuine/imposter/morph quadruplets from DCMorph [4]. Model-axis validation data. Annotated resources enter purely as validation ground truth, never as method input, each answering the one question it can honestly answer (CelebA [33]: cross-checks and scale, GAN-Control [42]: attribution/sensitivity and diagnosis, RFW [48] and the standard benchmarks: selection, CASIA-WebFace [53], DCMorph [4]: showcase). CelebA [33]: 202,599202{,}599 images, 10,17710{,}177 identities, 4040 binary attributes, re-aligned to the FR five-point 112×112112{\times}112 template. GAN-Control [42]: 1,0001{,}000 synthetic identities, each a base image plus 88 single-attribute traversals of 77 steps (55 generator-controlled, head orientation, age, hair color, illumination, expression, 33 low-level, brightness, hue, image quality, 57,00057{,}000 images), with 88 attribute-isolating protocols (7,0007{,}000 genuine pairs plus 7,0007{,}000 shared imposters each). RFW [48]: four ethnicity subsets, 6,0006{,}000 pairs each. Written attribute prompts. Validation exercises extensibility directly, writing one prompt or a few same-meaning phrasings per validated concept: one per CelebA attribute, 4141 across the 88 GAN-Control groups (group-averaging |Δ||\Delta|), three per RFW ethnicity, the prompt-only setting (3) adds small probed sets per variation axis (e.g. six age stages).

4.2 Vocabulary Projection as a Faithful Proxy for the FR

Table 1 instantiates the protocol of Section 3.5, row differences are attributable solely to the representations. Bounds. FR self-verification (row 1) sets the upper bound (97.44%97.44\% mean), the unaligned cross-encoder pairing (row 4) is the negative control at chance, 50.29%50.29\%, with near-zero TAR and rank-1 (SigLIP likewise, 50.70%50.70\%): independently trained spaces are empirically not comparable. The VLM encodes identity, the adapter reorganizes it. CLIP self-verification reaches 82.33%82.33\% despite never being trained for identity, and the adapter raises this to 92.58%92.58\% (+10.25+10.25, rows 2-3), SigLIP from 72.77%72.77\% to 84.78%84.78\% (+12.01+12.01, row 9). Since the adapter is a ≈1\approx\!1M-parameter MLP trained only to regress FR embeddings, the gain measures the identity structure recoverable from frozen VLM features. Alignment fidelity. In the aligned cross-encoder pairing (row 5) one image of every pair is encoded by gθ​(ϕv)g_{\theta}(\phi_{v}), the other by ψ\psi: 94.56%94.56\% mean, within 2.882.88 points of the upper bound. On template-based IJB-B/C the mixed pairing lands above the FR reference (96.6096.60/97.7097.70 vs. 95.5895.58/97.1897.18), plausibly because the regression objective smooths noisy low-quality embeddings toward identity-mean directions. The exception is TinyFace (13.49%13.49\% vs. 73.77%73.77\% rank-1), where the probes are extremely low-resolution. Extreme low resolution breaks the VLM’s image encoder, so every route through it breaks too. The signature takes no such route: it pairs ψ\psi’s embeddings with anchors built from text. Only row 8 and the VLM-proxy setting read images with the VLM, and only they degrade. Vocab. Proj. faithfulness and the contribution of cross-modal transfer. In CLIP’s native space, similarities to the 978978 prompts carry almost no identity information (row 6, 51.98%51.98\%), the identical vocabulary mapped by the image-trained adapter yields 71.66%71.66\% (row 7). Sharing prompts, VLM, and FR model, the +19.68+19.68-point gap isolates the cross-modal transfer, the component never directly supervised. Generality: four FR targets, two VLMs (Table 1, rows 9-17). With adapter architecture and training fixed and the FR target varying across two architecture families and two training sets, aligned-VLM self-verification stays within 0.710.71 points (91.8891.88-92.59%92.59\%): alignment fidelity is governed by the identity information in the frozen VLM features, not by the targeted FR geometry, so the adapter is a generic plug-in bridge. Vocab.-proj. faithfulness varies meaningfully instead, 75.18%75.18\% for ResNet-100/WebFace4M against 69.57%69.57\% for the same architecture on MS1MV2, a 5.615.61-point spread against near-identical upper bounds and alignment fidelity: different FR models expose different amounts of identity structure along nameable directions, and the vocabulary projection quantifies this per model. Swapping the VLM preserves the picture, CLIP giving the stronger image-side identity signal and SigLIP the stronger image-text coupling.

4.3 What Does the FR Model Keep? Selecting the Signature

Faithfulness as a whole does not license per-attribute claims: an anchor bank can retain identity information while individual anchors point away from their concepts, and the adapter maps the VLM’s modality gap into FR space rather than removing it, so per-attribute measurement uses the VLM-proxy anchors of Eq. 5. Detection over the whole vocabulary is anyway the wrong goal, since the FR model has erased some concepts on purpose. Detectability at vocabulary scale selects the signature. The measure of Section 3.3 runs on the adapter’s own identity holdout (10%10\% of WebFace4M identities). In VLM space every concept is self-consistently detectable (AUCV\mathrm{AUC}_{V} mean 0.9760.976, min 0.8770.877), in the adapter-mapped FR space detectability spreads widely (0.790.79-0.980.98), and the drop names what each model discounts (Figure 2a). Eyewear (0.9550.955), hair color (0.9470.947), hair style, and facial hair survive nearly intact, while distance (0.8530.853), scene context, camera angle, face coverings, and lighting are discounted most, largely capture conditions rather than the person. Discounted means not recoverable as a named direction, not invariance, since a mean-difference probe over VLM-defined groups can fail for either reason, we claim invariance only where behavior supports it, as for the photometric factors of Section 4.4, with lighting the counter-example, discounted here yet carrying real verification cost. The label-free AUCF\mathrm{AUC}_{F} predicts the labeled CelebA FR AUC of the matching attributes (ρ=0.43\rho=0.43-0.580.58 across targets, all p≤0.007p\leq 0.007) while the saturated AUCV\mathrm{AUC}_{V} predicts nothing: the FR-VLM difference carries the model-specific information. Because the pseudo-labels are the VLM’s own, a concept it cannot understand can still score high in both spaces, as head pose does (AUCF≈0.89\mathrm{AUC}_{F}\approx 0.89 although CLIP cannot rank real yaw), which is a limitation of EXPL-FR. Restricting to the top-mm attributes improves identity separability over the full vocabulary, scored on the signature (Figure 2b, top-mm vs. full at m=100m{=}100: 0.931/0.9100.931/0.910, 0.915/0.8980.915/0.898, 0.958/0.9400.958/0.940, 0.916/0.8980.916/0.898). We fix m=100m{=}100 as the semantic signature. Over the six model pairs, the selected top-100100 sets overlap at Jaccard 0.480.48-0.770.77, the two ViTs most alike: what FR training preserves is partly universal, partly model-specific. How much does the mapping flatter the FR model? AUCF\mathrm{AUC}_{F} is measured on adapter-mapped embeddings, not on real FR ones, so the structure it finds could come from the mapping rather than from the FR model. We extract true FR embeddings for the same 27,64827{,}648 holdout images and rescore the identical detector on them (AUCF∗\mathrm{AUC}_{F}^{*}, Figure 2a, diamonds), only the target space differs. The bias runs the other way: AUCF∗\mathrm{AUC}_{F}^{*} averages 0.7400.740 against AUCF\mathrm{AUC}_{F}’s 0.8940.894, a gap of 0.2360.236 from the VLM reference against the mapped measure’s 0.0820.082. Each measure shares a different amount of structure with the pseudo-labels, AUCV\mathrm{AUC}_{V} most and the independent FR encoder none, so both drops upper-bound the discount and neither level is absolute, the direction holds on all four targets, making our keep/discount picture conservative. The ordering the method is still valid: per-category ρ=0.63\rho=0.63-0.970.97 (n=22n{=}22), and within a model the two top-100100 sets overlap at Jaccard 0.560.56-0.790.79. Gender is the one substantive reordering, lowest under AUCF∗\mathrm{AUC}_{F}^{*} on three of four targets against its labeled CelebA score of 0.820.82. Labeled cross-check: anchor-attribute agreement. For each of the 4040 CelebA attributes and its written prompt, Figure 3a reports the AUC of a single coordinate separating label-positives from negatives, VLM-proxy anchors in FR space against VLM space (control). Identity-stable attributes score highest, led by blond hair at 0.890.89 (mean over all 4040: 0.640.64 primary, 0.610.61-0.650.65 across the four, VLM control 0.750.75), and the two-space comparison yields the same quadrant structure as detectability. High-VLM/attenuated-FR attributes are the discounted ones (e.g. eyeglasses, 0.97→0.500.97\to 0.50). Low/low attributes (e.g. bags-under-eyes 0.42/0.400.42/0.40) mark concepts the VLM cannot rank on aligned crops, which no construction rescues. Every prompt was written for its attribute rather than drawn from the vocabulary, turning extensibility into a measurement, phrasing matters predictably (negated concepts recover from below-chance to 0.740.74 FR/0.930.93 VLM when phrased positively with flipped sign), and the behavior is architecture-independent. Why do changeable attributes rank so high? The ranking puts hair color and eyewear above face shape and ethnicity, which looks backwards if it is read as saying which attributes make someone who they are. It says no such thing: stable attributes rank high too, gender at 0.820.82 and baldness at 0.750.75, alongside five-o’clock shadow at 0.770.77. Detectability asks only whether the FR space separates faces along one named direction. Fine facial geometry is encoded densely across many dimensions, so one linear coordinate captures little of it, and narrow eyes, high cheekbones, and bags under eyes sit at or below chance in both spaces (0.420.42-0.500.50), unmeasurable rather than unused. The high ranks, though, are genuine. In web-scraped training data a person’s photos usually show the same hair color, the same makeup habits, and glasses if they wear glasses, so these attributes predict identity and the model learns to use them. It then affects when they change: recoloring hair moves the embedding by 0.07-0.09, far more than the photometric factors it has erased. That dependence is a real weakness, and surfacing it is the audit working. Labeled cross-check: dependence ranking. Ranking concepts by how strongly they structure the FR space is the aggregate form of the same measurement, and Figure 3b validates it against [29]: per attribute, the macroscale distance-distribution KS statistic is computed twice on the same one-image-per-identity CelebA subsample, from label groups and from pseudo-labeled groups. The two agree at Spearman ρ=0.64\rho=0.64 (p=1.0×10−5p=1.0\times 10^{-5}, n=40n=40, 0.64/0.65/0.700.64/0.65/0.70 on the other targets, all p<10−4p<10^{-4}), with the label-dominant attributes (bald, blond hair, gray hair, male) recovered label-free: the analysis that required 4040 per-image annotations in [29] is reproducible from prompts alone. Controlled cross-check: attribution and sensitivity (500500 held-out GAN-Control identities, anchors from the other 500500). Attribution: the prompt group with the largest |Δ||\Delta| mass matches the varied attribute in 35%35\% of traversals (3535-37%37\% across targets, chance 1/81/8), a split the keep/discount picture predicts, since only kept attributes can be attributed. Encoded attributes attribute reliably (age 82%82\%, expression 75%75\%, hair color 64%64\%), whereas photometric ones land near chance with diffuse confusion rows because the FR embedding has erased them (genuine traversal pairs retain cosine 0.980.98-0.990.99). Orientation stays near chance for the opposite reason: the FR space demonstrably encodes pose (a labeled probe separates |yaw|≥30∘|\mathrm{yaw}|\geq 30^{\circ} at AUC 0.970.97) while CLIP cannot rank it on aligned 112×112112{\times}112 crops, so the anchors, not the FR model, are the weak link. Sensitivity: mean matched-group |Δ||\Delta| ranks the attributes consistently across all four models, age (0.220.22-0.260.26) ≫\gg hair color ≈\approx expression (0.070.07-0.090.09) >> orientation ≈\approx illumination >> image quality >> brightness >> hue, the ordering of [29]. Explaining data under a fixed FR model. Fixing the model, the signature explains data at three levels, shown in Figure 1b-d and described there: identity-wise profiles that are stable across capture conditions, per-image signatures, and differences over DCMorph [4] quadruplets in which the morph sits between genuine and imposter, its residual divergence naming the attributes inherited from the other contributor.

4.4 Can You Audit an FR Model Without Supervision?

We benchmark the settings end-to-end: three constructions, the same statistics, conditioned rank agreements. How does each model allocate its capacity? Figure 3c runs the dependence test over the full vocabulary for all four targets. All agree on what structures their spaces most, makeup, facial hair, gender, and hair color leading every profile [29], while the same ResNet-100 trained on MS1MV2 instead of WebFace4M shows uniformly weaker attribute structure, largest drops on ethnicity (0.045→0.0280.045\to 0.028), expression (0.035→0.0240.035\to 0.024), and facial hair (0.058→0.0400.058\to 0.040), naming the axes behind that pair’s 5.615.61-point faithfulness gap. Model selection without demographic labels (RFW). Per setting, a (model, group) pair’s audit value is the group’s KS dependence on the pooled ≈40,600\approx 40{,}600 unlabeled images, real behavior is the subset’s verification error. Figure 4: per group, the Kendall τ\tau between 4-model audit and real-error rankings averages 0.920.92 for all three settings (African, Caucasian, Indian at τ=1.0\tau=1.0, Asian 0.670.67). At n=4n{=}4 the exact permutation null gives p=0.042p=0.042 for a single τ=1.0\tau=1.0 and p=0.167p=0.167 for τ=0.67\tau=0.67, so no group is decisive alone, treating the four as independent tests puts the joint result at p=1.2×10−5p=1.2\times 10^{-5}. Ranking by mean dependence is moreover identical to ranking by mean real error under every setting: a model allocating more capacity to separating ethnicities is measurably the more biased, less accurate one, recovered from prompts and unlabeled faces alone. This confirms Figure 3c, where ethnicity was where the WebFace4M-vs-MS1MV2 pair diverged most. Selection on the standard benchmarks (age and pose). With probed prompt sets, setting (3) also ranks the models by their cross-age benchmark penalties (τ=+0.67\tau=+0.67 AgeDB-30, +0.33+0.33 CALFW): keep/discount showing up as behavior. If age still separates faces in a model’s embedding space, two photos of the same person years apart land further apart, so that model loses the most accuracy on the cross-age benchmarks. Pose is inconclusive (τ=0.00\tau=0.00 CFP-FP, −1.0-1.0 CPLFW, the two benchmarks disagreeing), because CLIP cannot comprehend pose on tightly aligned crops, so the adapter cannot map what the VLM does not encode and the pose axes track real yaw only weakly, yet the audit still returns systematic-looking values. Any audit of a concept the VLM cannot comprehend is therefore inconclusive. The two-space comparison flags such concepts as the low/low quadrant of Figure 3, but is not a complete screen: detectability alone scores pose at AUCF≈0.89\mathrm{AUC}_{F}\approx 0.89 because its pseudo-labels are the VLM’s own, so a blind spot can pass an unlabeled check and surface only against real behavior. We know of only two such blind spots, pose and illumination, so understanding of the VLM is a clear limitation. Model diagnosis under controlled variation (GAN-Control). Which variations will cost a fixed model? All four stay near ceiling under the eight attribute-isolating protocols (99.6599.65-100%100\%, expected on clean synthetic imagery), but the graded EER orders the variations: age is most expensive for every model, while brightness, hue, and image quality are behaviorally free (EER ≤0.014%\leq 0.014\%). Figure 4 (bottom) rank-correlates each setting’s per-attribute sensitivity against that ordering: primary target ρ=0.90/0.83/0.95\rho=0.90/0.83/0.95 (labeled / VLM-proxy / ours, n=8n=8, exact p=2.3×10−3/7.7×10−3/5.7×10−4p=2.3\times 10^{-3}/7.7\times 10^{-3}/5.7\times 10^{-4}), and across all four targets labeled 0.900.90-1.01.0, proxy 0.810.81-0.880.88, ours 0.690.69-0.950.95, the weakest still at p=0.035p=0.035. Even the prompts-only audit identifies which variations cost a model before any verification protocol is run. Illumination is the outlier, with real cost (EER 0.130.13-0.29%0.29\%) but no named-axis movement: like pose, a concept at the edge of the VLM’s range, not an FR invariance. Eight-way attribution degrades more sharply as supervision drops (labeled 8282-90%90\%, proxy 3333-34%34\%, ours 1616-19%19\%, chance 12.5%12.5\%), setting (3)’s weakest result, the proxy’s dip from Section 4.3’s 3535-37%37\% reflects one pseudo-labeled axis per attribute here versus 4141 group-averaged anchors there. Conversely GAN-Control cannot pose the selection question, since per-attribute EER sits at the floor for most variables, leaving models indistinguishable per attribute even when labeled, a limit of controlled-generator ground truth and hence of prior evaluations built on it [29]. Replacing supervised auditing at scale (CelebA). With no per-attribute behavior available, the reference is the supervised audit (1) itself. Within a model, the label-free dependence profile over the 4040 attributes correlates with the labeled one at ρ=0.26\rho=0.26-0.480.48 (proxy) and 0.210.21-0.510.51 (ours), against setting (1)’s own holdout self-consistency of 0.340.34-0.520.52, ours exceeds every setting on ResNet-100/MS1MV2 (0.510.51 vs. 0.480.48 proxy, 0.340.34 labeled). Per attribute, the 4-model ranking agrees with the supervised one at mean τ=0.63\tau=0.63 for the proxy (90%90\% of attributes consistent) and 0.450.45 for ours (78%78\%).

5 Conclusion

EXPL-FR grounds natural-language explanations in a frozen FR model’s own embedding space. An adapter trained on face images alone aligns a frozen VLM’s image encoder with the FR space and transfers unchanged to text, so an arbitrary vocabulary becomes a bank of candidate FR-space anchors, we measure that faithfulness of the transfer, with the same setting covering four FR targets and two VLMs. Because an FR model earns its invariances, only some concepts stay detectable after the mapping: a label-free measure selects each model’s identity-discriminating attributes, and the top-100100 form its semantic signature, separating identities better than the full vocabulary. Signatures explain images, identities, and genuine/imposter/morph pairs, and audit models under three benchmarked supervision settings. Selection survives even the prompts-only audit (τ=0.92\tau=0.92 on RFW), diagnosis stays informative in every setting, and CelebA quantifies the trade-off of dropping supervision (τ=0.45\tau=0.45 against the proxy’s 0.630.63), the cost of extending an audit by one written sentence. Limitations. The vocabulary: the FR-space projection stays 25.7825.78 points below the FR upper bound (Table 1, rows 1 vs. 7), some identity cues are not nameable, and prompts are not disentangled, so readings are directional. The VLM: every construction inherits what the VLM can rank on an image, and where it cannot, the audit still returns values that read like findings, as for pose, illumination, and extreme low resolution, such audits are inconclusive and the two-space comparison flags them only imperfectly. The measure: detectability is scored against the VLM’s own pseudo-labels and read through the adapter.

Appendix 0.A Supplementary Figures

This supplementary material accompanies the main paper. It collects the supporting figures: the supervision-setting overview (Fig. 5), differential-signature validation on GAN-Control traversals (Fig. 6), identity-wise signatures (Fig. 7), per-image semantic signatures on DCMorph quadruplets (Fig. 8), differential signatures on DCMorph quadruplets (Fig. 9), the standard-benchmark selection audit (Fig. 10), the CelebA at-scale comparison (Fig. 11), and the four-target diagnosis grid (Fig. 12). Figs. 13-16 extend the main paper’s primary-target analyses to all four FR targets: per-category detectability, CelebA anchor-attribute agreement, label-free dependence ranking, and GAN-Control attribution. Sec. 0.C collects the limitations. Sec. 0.G lists the candidate vocabulary and the written attribute prompts.

Appendix 0.B Per-Attribute Values and Between-Model Contrasts

Between-model sensitivity contrasts (GAN-Control, matched-group |Δ||\Delta|; complements main-paper Sec. 4.3). Between models, the ViTs move more along hair color than the ResNets (0.0850.085-0.0870.087 vs. 0.0670.067-0.0740.074), and ViT-B is the most age-invariant (0.2220.222 vs. 0.2480.248-0.2620.262).

All four targets. The primary-target analyses of main-paper Sec. 4.3 repeat on the remaining targets with the same structure: per-category detectability (Fig. 13), per-attribute anchor agreement on CelebA (Fig. 14), and the label-free dependence ranking (Fig. 15).

Appendix 0.C Limitations

Identity information outside the vocabulary. The FR-space vocabulary projection stays 25.7825.78 points below the FR upper bound (main-paper Table 1, rows 1 vs. 7): retained accuracy quantifies the identity structure expressible in K=978K{=}978 named directions, the gap what the vocabulary cannot express. Two properties of the vocabulary sit behind that gap. First, some identity cues may not be nameable at all. Fine, distributed facial geometry has no compact description in words, and one linear direction per prompt cannot capture it even where the model relies on it heavily, which is part of why such attributes rank low in main-paper Sec. 4.3. Second, the named directions are not mutually independent: a hair-style prompt also carries length, volume, and texture, and neighboring prompts within a category share variance, so per-attribute readings are directional rather than disentangled. Both are limits of the attribute vocabulary rather than of the alignment, but they bound how finely any prompt-based explanation can resolve.

The VLM bounds what can be measured, and its blind spots fail silently. Every anchor construction inherits what the VLM can rank on aligned 112×112112{\times}112 crops. Where it cannot rank a concept, the audit still returns values that read like findings. Four cases recur: pose (a labeled FR probe reaches AUC 0.970.97, yet CLIP cannot comprehend pose on aligned crops, so the adapter cannot transport it and pose audits are inconclusive, Sec. 0.E), illumination (real verification cost without named-axis movement), negated phrasings, and extreme low resolution (TinyFace, main-paper Sec. 4.2). All four are failures of the measurement, not FR invariances. Such blind spots are not knowable a priori. The two-space FR-vs-VLM comparison (main-paper Fig. 3a; Fig. 6) is the built-in diagnostic, and any audit of a concept it flags is inconclusive and must not be read as a finding.

Detectability rests on pseudo-labels, and is read through the adapter. Two dependencies limit how the detectability numbers may be read, and both trace back to the bullet above. First, the labels are the VLM’s, not ground truth. A concept’s positive and negative clouds are the extremes of the VLM’s own ranking, so AUCV\mathrm{AUC}_{V} is near-saturated by construction: it is measured in the space that generated the labels and mostly recovers them, which demonstrates self-consistency rather than that the VLM has grounded the concept in reality. We use it deliberately. Absent per-image labels, the VLM’s image-text coupling is the only mechanism for naming concepts at vocabulary scale, so it is the best reference available rather than a good one, and every caveat about the VLM’s competence propagates into the detectability numbers. Second, AUCF\mathrm{AUC}_{F} is read on adapter-mapped embeddings, which are a deterministic function of the embeddings that supplied the labels and inherit some of their structure, so it does not isolate the FR geometry either. Rescoring the identical detector on true FR embeddings for the same 27,64827{,}648 holdout images widens the gap roughly threefold (main-paper Sec. 4.3). Both gaps are therefore upper bounds on what the FR model discards, and the levels should not be read absolutely, but the direction is consistent on all four targets, so our keep/discount claims are conservative. What the method uses is the ordering, and that is preserved (ρ=0.63\rho=0.63-0.970.97 per target, and within a model the two measures’ top-100100 sets overlap at Jaccard 0.560.56-0.790.79, not to be confused with the between-model overlap quoted in Table 4); we keep AUCF\mathrm{AUC}_{F} as the criterion for the reason given in main-paper Sec. 3.3, that it ranks concepts by whether the anchors can reach them, not only by whether the FR space separates them. Gender is the one category that changes standing between the two measures, on three of the four targets, and we have no account of it.

Limits of the ground truth, not the audit. Four constraints come from the validation resources themselves. GAN-Control’s per-attribute EER saturates (≤0.014%\leq 0.014\% for most variables), so no method, the labeled one included, can rank models per attribute there; any FR auditing evaluation built on controlled generators inherits this, prior practice included. Its age traversals also partially exit the identity (endpoint cosine 0.550.55-0.590.59 against ≈0.79\approx 0.79 overall), which makes the age sensitivity an upper bound that conflates attribute change with identity drift. RFW derives from MS-Celeb-1M, so the MS1MV2 target is partly in-domain there, likely contributing to its leading accuracy independently of its low dependence. Finally, every model-ranking statistic runs over n=4n=4 models, and within-model per-group rankings on RFW (n=4n=4 groups) are accordingly noisy for the label-free settings.

Alignment-data mismatch. All adapters are aligned on WebFace4M, so part of the MS1MV2 target’s lower signature faithfulness (69.57%69.57\% vs. 75.18%75.18\% for the same architecture on WebFace4M) may reflect the distribution mismatch between its training data and our alignment data rather than its geometry alone.

Appendix 0.D Explaining Data Under a Fixed FR Model

With the signature faithful and selected, we turn to the first analysis axis under a fixed model (AdaFace ViT-B / WebFace4M, CLIP anchors; row-7 configuration).

Identity-wise: profiles are aggregated over 5050 images for each of five CASIA-WebFace identities (Fig. 7). They are markedly identity-specific, each identity concentrating its strongest activations in a different category subset (e.g. ID 003879 is dominated by eyewear prompts), and the concentration persists across all 5050 capture conditions. This is an identity-level explanation: it names the attribute directions along which the model consistently encodes a person, rather than properties of one photograph.

Differential, on morphing quadruplets: a morph blends two source identities into one face designed to verify against both contributors. Each DCMorph case provides a reference, a genuine image of the same identity, an imposter, and a morph of the reference with that imposter (Fig. 9). Reference-genuine differences are near-uniformly small, reflecting within-identity stability. Reference-imposter differences are large and concentrated in specific semantic categories, naming the axes that separate the identities. The reference-morph difference is consistently smaller than reference-imposter, and closer in both magnitude and structure to reference-genuine. The morph therefore retains a substantial share of the reference’s identity semantics, the property that makes morphing attacks succeed, while its residual, category-concentrated divergence names the attributes inherited from the other contributor. The differential signature thus refines a scalar match score into a per-attribute account of where a morph borrows from each source.

Appendix 0.E Selection on the Standard Benchmarks

AgeDB-30 and CALFW vary age; CFP-FP and CPLFW vary pose. Setting (3) is therefore testable on ground truth every practitioner already trusts. Two graduated prompt sets, six age stages and a fresh three-prompt frontal-to-profile pose set, audit each model’s dependence on an independent unlabeled pool (pooled RFW; CelebA agrees in sign). Each audit is compared against the benchmark’s penalty, its error minus the same model’s LFW error, which isolates the cost of the variation from overall model quality.

Fig. 10: the age audit ranks the models as their cross-age penalties do (τ=+0.67\tau=+0.67 AgeDB-30, +0.33+0.33 CALFW), label-free and without touching a benchmark image. Pose is inconclusive (τ=−1.0\tau=-1.0 CPLFW, 0.000.00 CFP-FP). The model with the lowest pose audit value, ResNet-100/MS1MV2, pays the largest CPLFW penalty, while CFP-FP shows no agreement at all.

We attribute this to the audit’s VLM bound rather than to the models. CLIP cannot comprehend pose on tightly aligned 112×112112{\times}112 crops (main-paper Sec. 4.3), so the adapter cannot transport what the VLM does not encode. The pose-axis projection tracks real |yaw||\mathrm{yaw}| only weakly within identity (mean ρ=+0.11\rho=+0.11 to +0.34+0.34 on GAN-Control, against a labeled FR probe at AUC 0.970.97), enough residual correlation to produce systematic-looking rankings but not to support them. Two pose benchmarks contradicting each other is exactly what an audit running outside the VLM’s competence looks like. Any audit of a concept the VLM cannot comprehend is therefore inconclusive (Sec. 0.C). Without prior knowledge of the blind spot, the CPLFW inversion would be accepted as a finding, and the two-space FR-vs-VLM comparison of main-paper Sec. 4.3 is the diagnostic that flags such concepts before any audit is read. The age panels show the same audit where the VLM can rank the concept.

Appendix 0.F Attribution and Sensitivity Under Controlled Variation

Fig. 6, with per-target confusions in Fig. 16, on 500500 held-out GAN-Control identities with anchors built from the other 500500.

Attribution: the written prompt group with the largest |Δ||\Delta| mass matches the varied attribute in 35%35\% of traversals (3535-37%37\% across targets; chance 1/8=12.5%1/8=12.5\%, all eight attributes competing). That aggregate hides a sharp split. Encoded attributes are attributed reliably (age 82%82\%, expression 75%75\%, hair color 64%64\%). The photometric attributes (brightness, hue, image quality) land near chance with diffuse confusion rows, because the FR embedding has largely erased them (genuine traversal pairs retain cosine 0.980.98-0.990.99), which is the invariance a good FR model must have. Orientation also stays near chance, but for the opposite reason. The FR space demonstrably encodes pose, since a labeled linear probe separates |yaw|≥30∘|\mathrm{yaw}|\geq 30^{\circ} at AUC 0.970.97, while CLIP cannot rank pose on tightly aligned 112×112112{\times}112 crops: the pose anchors, not the FR model, are the weak link.

Sensitivity: mean matched-group |Δ||\Delta| ranks the attributes consistently across all four models, age (0.2220.222-0.2620.262) ≫\gg hair color (0.0670.067-0.0870.087) ≈\approx expression (0.0710.071-0.0840.084) >> orientation ≈\approx illumination (0.0400.040-0.0430.043) >> image quality (≈0.019\approx 0.019) >> brightness (0.0120.012-0.0140.014) >> hue (0.0070.007). Between-model contrasts are collected in Sec. 0.B.

Appendix 0.G The Semantic Vocabulary and Written Attribute Prompts

Table 5 lists the candidate vocabulary of main-paper Sec. 4.1: K=978K{=}978 prompts in M=22M{=}22 disjoint categories, each instantiating the template “A photo of …” with a single attribute value. The complete prompt lists ship with the code. The audits additionally use written attribute prompts, never drawn from this vocabulary (main-paper Sec. 4.1): one per CelebA attribute (4040, with negated concepts phrased positively and the sign flipped), 4141 across the 88 GAN-Control groups, and three phrasings per RFW ethnicity (e.g. “A photo of a person of European descent.”). Setting (3) uses small graduated sets per variation axis instead: six age stages from “A photo of a baby.” to “A photo of an elderly person.”, ordered pose phrasings (frontal →\to three-quarter →\to profile), and per-variable level sets for GAN-Control.
